title: World War I: Trench Warfare and South Africa
summary: Trench warfare and new weapons on the Western Front, South Africa's involvement including the sinking of the SS Mendi, the end of the war and the Treaty of Versailles.

notes.text: Trench warfare on the Western Front

After the German advance was stopped in France in September 1914, both sides dug **trenches**. A line of trenches stretched about 700 km from the Belgian coast to Switzerland: the **Western Front**. The land between opposing trenches was called **no man's land**, full of barbed wire, mud and shell craters.

items: Soldiers lived in wet, muddy trenches with rats, lice and the smell of death.
Standing in water caused **trench foot**; diseases spread quickly.
Attacks meant going 'over the top' into machine-gun fire. Huge numbers died for a few hundred metres of land.
At the **Battle of the Somme** (1916) Britain lost almost 60 000 casualties on the first day alone.

notes.caption: New weapons
rows: Fired hundreds of bullets a minute; made attacks across open ground deadly
Caused most casualties; constant shelling caused 'shell shock' (trauma)
Blinded, burned and choked soldiers; gas masks were developed
Could cross trenches and barbed wire; later helped to break the stalemate
First used for scouting, then for dogfights and bombing
German submarines sank Allied ships to cut off supplies

notes.title: Why did the front barely move?
notes.problem: Explain why trench warfare led to stalemate.
steps: Machine guns and artillery made attacks over open ground deadly.
Defenders could bring up reinforcements faster than attackers could advance.
notes.answer: Weapons favoured defence, so neither side could break through.

notes.text: As part of the British Empire, the **Union of South Africa** was at war when Britain declared war. Prime Minister **Louis Botha** and **Jan Smuts** supported Britain. Some Afrikaners who opposed fighting for Britain staged the **1914 Rebellion**, which was put down.

items: **German South West Africa** (Namibia): South African forces conquered it in 1915; South Africa later governed it.
**German East Africa** (Tanzania): Smuts led a long campaign from 1916.
**Western Front**: the South African Brigade fought at **Delville Wood** (July 1916), where most of the 3 000 soldiers were killed, wounded or captured in six days of fighting.

Black South Africans were not allowed to carry weapons; about 25 000 served in the **South African Native Labour Contingent** (SANLC) in France, loading ships and building roads and railways. Coloured soldiers served in the Cape Corps.

notes.text: The sinking of the SS Mendi

On **21 February 1917** the troopship **SS Mendi**, carrying members of the SANLC to France, was struck in thick fog off the Isle of Wight by a larger ship, the SS Darro. More than **600 South Africans** died. According to survivors, **Reverend Isaac Wauchope Dyobha** calmed the men on the sinking ship.

notes.title: Source E: The words attributed to Rev. Isaac Wauchope Dyobha (adapted)
notes.text: Be quiet and calm, my countrymen. What is happening now is what you came to do. You are going to die, but that is what you came to do. Brothers, we are drilling the death drill.

The black labourers received no war medals from the government, unlike white soldiers. Their sacrifice was largely ignored until after 1994; today South Africa's highest award for bravery is the **Order of Mendi for Bravery**, and the SAS Isaac Dyobha is named after the minister.

notes.title: Why it is remembered
notes.problem: Why is the sinking of the Mendi on 21 February 1917 important in South African memory?
steps: More than 600 members of the South African Native Labour Corps died when the ship was struck in fog in the English Channel.
Black South Africans served without weapons, and their service received little recognition.
The Mendi has become a symbol of sacrifice and of injustice.
notes.answer: It honours men whose sacrifice was long ignored because of racism.

items: The USA joined the Allies in 1917; Russia left the war after its revolution.
Germany signed an **armistice** (ceasefire) on **11 November 1918** at 11 a.m.

The **Treaty of Versailles** (1919) blamed Germany for the war (the 'war guilt' clause), forced it to pay huge **reparations**, limited its army and took away its colonies. Many Germans resented the treaty, which helped lead to World War II.
The **League of Nations** was set up to keep peace in future.
